summary: Redwood ran an Optimize walkthrough focused on batching strategies (static batching vs streaming continuous batching) and prefix/KV cache recommendations for Petrichor's sessioned conversational product. Discussed tradeoffs between latency and unit-cost, sample cost model showing ~28-40% cost reduction with KV prefetch + session affinity on their traffic shape. Agreed next steps: share runbook and spreadsheet, run a latency SLO sim, and provision a short Dedicated trial for benchmarking.
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: hi everyone thanks for joining, i'm sofia from Redwood, we'll run through an optimize / batching + kv strategy walkthrough, please say hi
[00:06] Lena: hey hi, lena here, excited to see the numbers, we've got about 10 minutes to cover current constraints then deep dive
[00:12] Marcus: tom and i will watch, i'll drop a traffic histogram in chat after
[00:18] Daniel: cool, quick agenda, 1) traffic profile review, 2) batching options and latency/cost simulations, 3) prefix kv strategies and prefetch, 4) recommended config & next steps
[00:28] Priya: just to flag our top goals: <95ms p95 for short prompts, keep CPU/GPU costs budget under $X per 1M requests, and avoid GPL data egress for PII
[00:37] Sofia: understood — we tuned the cost model to those SLOs, i'll call out assumptions as we go, some numbers are ballpark until we get your exact session histogram
[00:45] Daniel: ok jumping in — first slide: your traffic is highly sessionized, about 18k daily active sessions, median session length approx 4 exchanges, tail long with some 50+ message sessions. that shape favors prefix caching and session-affinity to capture hot KV state
[01:05] Marcus: small note, our sessions have frequent system messages and long prefix tokens — sometimes 300 tokens per context
[01:12] Daniel: yep that matters, token-length distribution increases KV size, affects warm cache eviction and quantization choices, we call this out in the runbook
[01:22] Sofia: next: batching — we compared two runtime modes: static batching where requests are batched at fixed intervals (e.g., 20ms flush) vs streaming/continuous batching that collects and emits as soon as batch fills or when headroom reached
[01:36] Daniel: static batching gives predictable throughput and higher batch sizes which reduces per-token GPU time, but adds baseline latency. streaming reduces tail latency for single-user interactions at cost of smaller batches
[01:49] Lena: can you show numbers? what's the tradeoff for our 95ms target?
[01:54] Daniel: yes, we ran a sim with your qps and session mix. baseline (no cache, static batch 20ms) gave p95 ~120ms and unit cost X. switching to streaming batching with 8-12 ms flush gets p95 to ~92ms but cost increases ~12% because batch efficiency lower. combine streaming + prefix KV prefetch, p95 ~88ms and cost drops below baseline by ~28% because we saved decoding tokens via cache hits
[02:24] Priya: wait, how are you computing the 28%? that sounds high
[02:28] Sofia: good callout — it's aggregated: 18% from prefix KV hit-rate (we assumed 46% hit-rate on your session prefixes), 10% from reduced decoder tokens (we avoid regenerating repeated system + user history thanks to prefix cache). the model assumes average prefix length 220 tokens and a cache hit avoids those tokens being re-decoded
[02:50] Tom: is that realistic for our customers? we saw prefixes shift between conversations alot
[02:55] Daniel: it's sticky if you use session-affinity and prefetch on session start. we recommend prefetch policy: on session start, prefetch top-2 prefixes for the last 5 messages, warm KV locally on the serving GPU. for sessions with >80% repeated system tokens, hit rates approach 60% in our benchmarks
[03:17] Marcus: how big is the KV per session with those tokens? memory implications matter for Dedicated pools
[03:23] Daniel: good point — with 220-token prefixes token-emb size and kv requires ~1.2MB per active session in our runtime (with 8-bit quant and overheads). with 18k sessions that would be huge so we recommend session eviction policy + LRU per-GPU and an optional prefix-store (SSD-backed) for cold sessions
[03:40] Priya: so memory per session is non-trivial. do you have guidance to set eviction thresholds?
[03:45] Daniel: yes we typically set warm KV cap per-GPU to cover 500-1,000 hot sessions depending on traffic; everything else is on-disk and fetched on demand with async prefetch to avoid blocking first prompt
[03:55] Sofia: next slide: cost model inputs — we used your qps: 80 rps peak, avg payload tokens 180, session ratio, and 95ms p95 target. we'll show alternate knobs: increase batch window to 25ms to save cost but p95 goes to ~110ms
[04:10] Lena: can you run the sim with longer prefixes? ours sometimes go to 400 tokens
[04:15] Daniel: yes we have that scenario — longer prefixes increase KV size but also increase benefit of cache hits; in a 400 token prefix scenario hit reduces token decode up to 45% so net cost improvement can be even better, but memory pressure increases
[04:28] Marcus: what about concurrent requests per session? we have some background async requests that can inflate concurrency
[04:34] Daniel: concurrency matters a lot — if concurrency per-session >1 you get natural batching and higher efficiency. our cost model includes a concurrency multiplier; for your traffic if background async makes concurrency 1.3x, cost per request drops ~7% with same latency
[04:50] Sofia: switching to prefix fetch strategies — we demo three patterns: on-demand fetch, opportunistic prefetch, and eager session prefetch. each has tradeoffs on cold-start latency, memory, and network IO
[05:03] Daniel: on-demand: smallest memory, highest cold-start latency. opportunistic: prefetch on tail of user activity, best balance. eager: prefetch entire session history at session start, high memory but best steady-state p95
[05:15] Lena: what does console support look like — can we tune policies per-route?
[05:19] Amira: yes in Redwood Console Optimize panel, you can define per-endpoint prefetch policies, retention windows, batch-flush ms, and per-route SLOs. we also show estimated cost delta as you change knobs
[05:31] Priya: will we be able to A/B different configs and collect production hit-rates?
[05:36] Sofia: yes, rollouts and metrics are built-in, you can run canary with 10% traffic and compare tokens saved, p95, and cost. Optimize will surface regression alerts if quality drops below thresholds on prompt sets
[05:48] Marcus: security: how is KV material stored? we have PII and must use customer-managed keys
[05:54] Daniel: KV in Redwood Private or Dedicated can be encrypted with your KMS/HSM. the control plane never sees plaintext for Private deployments; we have an integration doc (we'll share) and audit logs for read/write events
[06:06] Tom: does prefetch increase our compliance risk due to preloading user data?
[06:10] Sofia: policy-wise you can configure prefetch to only include non-sensitive system tokens, or redact sensitive fields before storing in KV. we recommend a transformation pipeline at ingestion for PII handling
[06:21] Lena: back to numbers — can you show a sample run of the console sim now?
[06:26] Daniel: sure, sharing screen — here's the Optimize tab, i uploaded a sample traffic dump (synthetic) matching petrichor histogram. top-left: batch window slider — moving from 8ms to 25ms updates estimated cost and p95 in real time
[06:40] [screen share noise — garbled for a few seconds]
[06:48] Daniel: ok apologies, small audio glitch. so with these inputs: streaming mode, batch flush 10ms, prefetch eager for session start, kv hit-rate 52% estimated, p95 86ms, unit cost $0.62 per 1k tokens (example) — baseline was $0.88 per 1k tokens without caching
[07:07] Priya: that's a meaningful saving. are these numbers for Hosted or Dedicated?
[07:11] Daniel: these are for Hosted with our recommended runtime. Dedicated often has slightly lower per-token nodes but you pay for reserved capacity; in Dedicated, with similar config we estimate $0.48 per 1k tokens on the same GPU fleet due to better amortization
[07:26] Marcus: that delta suggests Dedicated might be worth it if we hit our projected qps, what thresholds do you recommend?
[07:32] Sofia: rule of thumb: if sustained qps > 2-3K tokens/sec for prolonged periods and predictable growth, Dedicated becomes cost-effective. we can run a cost curve for your forecast numbers — we'll add to the spreadsheet
[07:46] Lena: what about fallbacks if cache misses spike or prefix patterns change quickly? we need graceful degradation
[07:52] Daniel: Redwood has policy-based fallback: if KV miss-rate crosses a threshold, runtime switches to best-effort batching mode and temporarily increases batch windows to preserve throughput, plus can route to alternative smaller model variants for cost control while preserving functionality
[08:07] Tom: model variants and routing — is that per-tenant? can we set per-customer policies?
[08:12] Amira: yes per-tenant routing is supported, you can pin routes to dedicated pools or route to cheaper variants under load. policies are expressed in the Console as JSON rules or via a policy UI
[08:22] Marcus: latency for primary decoder on fallback — any numbers?
[08:25] Daniel: typical fallback to smaller variant increases p95 by ~45-70ms depending on model family; we surface this in simulation before rollout so you can decide tradeoffs
[08:36] Priya: curious about quantization impact on KV size and hit-rate — do you degrade quality?
[08:41] Daniel: 8-bit quant keeps decode fidelity high for most open models; KV representation uses quantized keys and tends not to affect similarity matching if your embeddings are normalized. we log any quality regressions during A/B and rollback if needed
[08:55] Sofia: quick pause — any blockers from legal/security on prefetch or storing session state?
[08:59] Priya: legal flagged data residency for EU; some sessions will be EU-only, need on-prem or VPC in eu-west-1 for those tenants
[09:06] Sofia: we have Private deployment options and region routing; we'll include architecture note for region-restricted tenants in the runbook
[09:13] Lena: ok now the more tactical config we might adopt — recommended starter config for you: streaming batching, 10ms flush, eager prefetch for sessions with >3 messages, warm-KV cap 800 per GPU, LRU evict 30m, async SSD-prefetch for cold sessions, and canary rollout 5-10%
[09:36] Marcus: sounds good, please include expected memory footprint and cost delta per config in the spreadsheet
[09:41] Sofia: noted — that's part of deliverables
[09:44] Daniel: quick demo: i toggled prefetch aggressiveness to medium and the console showed estimated token savings drop from 38% to 22% but memory usage halved. tradeoff screen pops useful charts
[09:58] Lena: do you capture example prompts that failed semantic parity after caching? want to see edge cases
[10:03] Daniel: yes Optimize can run differential evals with your testset and report semantic differences. we sample both cached and non-cached outputs and compute fidelity metrics. if we see drift we'll back off caching for that prefix pattern
[10:18] Priya: good. who will run initial pilot and own it?
[10:22] Marcus: we'll nominate an owner internally, likely platform, but ML will own cache logic decisions
[10:28] Sofia: to wrap up — recap: we'll send runbook, cost spreadsheet, SOC2/KMS notes; Daniel will prepare a latency sim with your real histogram; you’ll provide exported session histogram and any PII redaction rules
[10:41] Lena: timeline: we want bench results by 10/30 and decision on Dedicated by 11/10 if numbers align
[10:48] Sofia: sounds realistic, we'll do that. any final q's?
[10:52] Tom: one last: for on-prem Private, is there an air-gap deployment option?
[10:56] Daniel: yes we offer an on-prem package with an offline installer and airgap instructions; that's a separate engagement but feasible
[11:04] Priya: ok thanks everyone, useful session
[11:07] Sofia: thanks all, will follow up shortly with assets
[11:10] [meeting ends]
